title: Overview
summary: LexGraph is a governed semantic layer over both database tables and documents. Its single organising commitment is that every fact it holds carries a record of how it came to be believed — so that question always has a real answer, not a plausible one.

headings.text: The value proposition, in one paragraph
The five classes, at a glance

body: Overview Why does the system believe this? LexGraph is a governed semantic layer over both database tables and documents. Its single organising commitment is that every fact it holds carries a record of how it came to be believed — so that question always has a real answer, not a plausible one. What it is LexGraph sits between a firm's data and the people asking it questions. Underneath are two kinds of source: structured data (database tables reached through AWS Glue and Athena) and unstructured data (documents — filings, contracts, opinions, correspondence). On top is a knowledge graph of entities and the relationships between them, plus a set of approved metric definitions. What makes it different from a search box or a chatbot over the same data is that nothing enters the graph anonymously. Each relationship — each edge — is an assertion: a claim recorded alongside how it was arrived at, what it rests on, how confident the system is, when it was learned, who has signed it off, and which firm it belongs to. There is exactly one function in the codebase that can create one, and it refuses to create an incomplete one. The consequence is that a user can always ask a follow-up question that most systems cannot answer: where did that come from? For a fact read from a document, the answer is a file, a page, and the sentence itself. For a fact a rule worked out, the answer is a proof tree that unwinds to the documents and records at its base. Who it is for LexGraph is built as a whitelabel platform for legal AI products. Three audiences use it, and the documentation tries to serve all three: Lawyers and analysts Ask questions, read the answer, and check the citation. The pages worth reading are Asking questions, Provenance and the Glossary. Administrators and risk Set the trust thresholds, run the review queue, operate the ethical walls. See Governance settings, Reviewing claims and Tenancy and ethical walls. Technical evaluators Judge whether the guarantees are real. Start with The assertion contract, then How extraction works and Architecture. The platform is domain-agnostic by construction. It reads a vocabulary pack that names the entities, relationships and rules of a domain; the legal pack is simply the default. A second pack for healthcare ships alongside it, not because healthcare is a target market but because a single-pack abstraction rots quietly and a second one makes the rot visible in a test rather than in a customer's deployment. The value proposition, in one paragraph In one paragraph Any competent system can find a passage in a document and put a sentence in front of a lawyer. What a regulated buyer needs, and what nothing on the market reliably provides, is the ability to say which of its beliefs are mechanically checkable, which rest on a model's judgement, which were derived by a rule from other beliefs, and which are outright guesses — and to keep those categories apart at the moment a question is answered rather than in a report afterwards. LexGraph makes that distinction the primary key of its data model. A fact that a string search confirmed is on page 7 is a different kind of object from a model's view that one holding undercuts another, and the system will not let them be mistaken for each other. Everything else — the review queue, the ethical walls, the trust thresholds, the four-tier read path — follows from that one decision. The five classes, at a glance "Epistemic" means "to do with knowledge". That is the last time this documentation uses the word without a plainer one alongside. The epistemic class of a fact is how the system came to believe it, and it is one of five: Class How it was reached Does a person sign it off? DECLARED A system of record said so — a case management export, a scan of the data catalogue. No. It is true by definition of the source. EXTRACTED_DET A quoted sentence was claimed to be on a named page, and a search of that page confirmed the words are there. No. The check is repeatable, so there is nothing for a person to add. EXTRACTED_MODEL Something read into the document rather than merely found in it. Yes. This is the only class the review queue exists for. INFERRED A rule derived it from other facts, which it names as its premises. Yes, and its proof tree can be opened. PREDICTED A statistical guess from the shape of the graph. No document says it. Never used in an answer at all unless explicitly asked for. Without this axis, a citation parsed out of a filing and a language model's opinion are both just edges in a graph, indistinguishable at the moment somebody asks a question. The assertion contract covers all five in full, along with the five invariants the system enforces and why review state is derived rather than chosen. How a question is answered Questions are resolved by trying four routes in order, most precise first, and the route that succeeded is reported back as part of the answer. That is not an implementation detail leaking out: "this came from an approved metric" and "a model wrote this SQL" are different claims about how much the number can be trusted, and the person reading it is entitled to know which one they have. 1 Governed metric A metric definition matched the question and compiled to SQL. No model was involved in producing the query. The same question returns the same SQL every time. 2 Graph traversal The answer came from walking assertions that clear the trust threshold and that this user is allowed to see. Every fact in the answer is a cited assertion you can open. 3 Hybrid Relevant passages were retrieved by similarity, then expanded along verified relationships out from them. Sources are cited; the expansion only follows trusted edges. 4 Generated SQL No approved metric matched, so a model wrote SQL against the real schema. It is checked by a query firewall before running. Not a governed answer. An administrator can switch this tier off entirely. Asking questions explains what each tier means for trust, and the kill switch that turns the fourth one off. What is not built yet This documentation describes a system in active development, and it is more useful to be honest about the gaps than to describe an intention as a feature. The significant ones: Honest gaps There is no reasoning engine. The INFERRED class, the premise structure, the proof-tree machinery and the confidence ceiling on inferences are all built and tested, and two rules are written out in the legal vocabulary pack. Nothing fires them: no code path passes INFERRED to build_assertion, so the rules are listed to callers and never evaluated. Until something fires them, no inferred facts exist in practice — which means the conflict check and the stale-authority check are the two things this system most wants to demonstrate and cannot yet. Assertions are not persisted. This remains the single largest gap. They live in an in-process store, so they do not survive a restart or a deploy, and the read path reads from that store rather than from the graph. Neptune is connected and its schema, indexes and scoped reads all work — governed metrics and their version history really are written to and read from the graph — but no writer puts assertions there. Everything else durable is genuinely durable: documents in S3, ingest jobs and matter grants in DynamoDB, metric definitions in Neptune. Tier 4 has no SQL generator wired up, so in practice it always declines. The query firewall it would be checked against does exist and is tested. Tier 1 returns SQL but not a result. The Athena executor is written and tested, including the firewall check inside it, but nothing connects it to the metric path, so a governed metric compiles to SQL that is never run. Vector search is in-process. The managed search service is provisioned and its endpoint is passed to the application, but no adapter has been written against it, so embeddings are held in the task's memory and lost on restart. Per-tenant governance settings are in-process too, so a change made in Admin is lost on the next deploy. Relatedly, the blocked-questions list an administrator reads is always empty: refusals are recorded per request and never accumulated, so the kill switch refuses correctly but cannot show you what it refused. One task only. Live ingest progress arrives over a WebSocket served by a single process, and ingestion itself runs as a background task inside the API container, so it dies with the container. The durable job store makes a failed run retryable, not resumable. The 30-second poll, not the socket, is the correctness guarantee. Deployment is no longer among them: all six stacks — LexGraphNetwork, LexGraphData, LexGraphAuth, LexGraphApp, LexGraphMcp and LexGraphWeb — are applied to a real account, and the document pipeline runs there end to end: a presigned browser upload lands in S3, a notification starts ingestion, and pages are transcribed, chunked, embedded and read by a model. Where a page describes something in this list, it says so at that point rather than leaving the reader to check here. A note on these documents This site explains why the system is shaped the way it is, not only what it does. Several of the most instructive entries record a decision that was reversed: the character offsets that were demoted, the pattern-matching extractor that was deleted outright, the structural tenant isolation that turned out not to exist in the database being used. In each case the reversal is more useful than the conclusion, because the reasoning that led into the mistake is easy to repeat. The documentation is written to agree with the code, and where the two disagreed while this was being written, the code won and the difference is noted. It reuses the application's own plain-language wording wherever the application has any, so the tooltip a user sees in the product and the explanation here do not drift apart.

title: The assertion contract
summary: Every relationship in the graph is an assertion, and there is one function that can create one. That is what makes the guarantees on this page hold for the whole system rather than for the code paths somebody remembered to check.

headings.text: Why review state is derived, not chosen
Two gates that are easily confused
How this is stored, and why it is denormalised

body: Start here The assertion contract Every relationship in the graph is an assertion, and there is one function that can create one. That is what makes the guarantees on this page hold for the whole system rather than for the code paths somebody remembered to check. src/graph/assertions.py What an assertion is A knowledge graph is entities joined by relationships. "Counsel Smith represents Acme Corp" is a relationship between two entities. In most systems that is the whole of it: a line connecting two dots, perhaps with a confidence number attached. In LexGraph the same relationship is an assertion, and it carries: Field What it records tenant_id Which firm this belongs to. Never optional. subject, predicate, object The claim itself: who, what relationship, to whom. epistemic_class How the system came to believe it. One of five; see below. method The specific, versioned thing that produced it — a named model, a rule with its version, a catalogue scan. confidence A number from 0 to 1 for this one fact. source_locator Where it came from, precisely enough to check by hand. For a document: the file, the page, and the quoted sentence. premises For a derived fact, the facts it was derived from. Unwinds into a proof tree. rule_id, rule_version Which rule derived it, if a rule did. valid_from, valid_until World time — the period during which the fact was actually true. recorded_at, superseded_at Transaction time — when the system learned it, and when it stopped believing it. review_state Whether a person has signed it off. Derived, not chosen — see below. matter_id Which matter it belongs to, if any. This is what an ethical wall filters on. Two clocks rather than one is worth pausing on. World time is when something was true; transaction time is when the system found out. Keeping both is what makes "what did the file show on the date we advised?" answerable — a real requirement in legal work, and one that is brutal to retrofit, because the information simply was not captured. The identifier of an assertion is a hash of its own content, which has a useful consequence: re-ingesting the same document produces the same identifiers and therefore changes nothing. The method is part of that hash, so re-extracting with an improved extractor produces new assertions that supersede the old generation rather than colliding with it. The five classes This is the axis the whole design turns on. Without it, a citation parsed out of a filing and a language model's opinion are both simply edges, and there is no way to tell them apart at the moment somebody asks a question. DECLARED A system of record said so — a case management export, a scan of the data catalogue. Not inferred and not extracted from prose. If the source says it, it is true by definition of the source; if it is wrong, the source is wrong. Enters the graph without review. EXTRACTED_DET A claim that a deterministic check confirmed. Note carefully what this does and does not mean, because the name is misleading if you assume the obvious reading. It does not mean "a regular expression found it". There is no pattern-matching layer in the system at all. What it means is: a model proposed that some text appears on some page, and a string search against that page either confirmed the words are there or it did not. The proposal is probabilistic. The confirmation is not, and the confirmation is what the class records. Only presence claims can qualify, because presence is the only thing such a check can establish. "This quote appears on page 7" is verifiable. "This holding undercuts that argument" is not. How extraction works covers this in full — it is the most important idea in the system and the easiest to misread. EXTRACTED_MODEL A model's interpretation, which nothing can mechanically confirm. Everything semantic lands here: whether a citation was relied on or distinguished, whether one clause supersedes another, whether a party is adverse to another. This is the class the review queue exists for, and separating it from verified presence is what keeps that queue small enough to actually be read. INFERRED Derived by a rule from other assertions. It carries its premises — the facts it rests on — so it can always be explained as a proof tree, and so that retracting a premise retracts the conclusion. Not built yet No reasoning engine is wired up. The class, the premise structure, the proof-tree plumbing and the confidence ceiling below are all built and tested, and two rules are written out in the legal vocabulary pack (a conflict check and a stale-authority check). Nothing currently fires them, so in practice no inferred assertions exist. PREDICTED A statistical guess from the shape of the graph — the kind of suggestion a link-prediction model makes. Nobody asserted it and no document says it. It is a research hint, never a finding, and it is excluded from answers entirely unless a caller explicitly opts in to seeing suggestions. The exclusion is enforced in the scoping layer rather than left to each screen, and a caller who passes the class in explicitly still does not get it without the flag. The five enforced invariants These are checked by the single function that builds assertions. Each one is cheap to enforce at that boundary and expensive or impossible to bolt on later. 1. Attribution is mandatory A tenant, a method, and a source locator are all required. An unattributed edge is not defensible, and a system whose purpose is to answer "why do you believe this?" cannot hold facts that have no answer. The method must be specific and versioned — llm:claude-sonnet-5, rule:conflict_check@v2, glue:catalog_scan — so that improving a producer supersedes its old output instead of silently mixing generations. 2. An inference must name its premises A derived fact with no stated basis cannot be explained, and it cannot be retracted correctly either: nothing knows to withdraw it when the thing it rested on is withdrawn. So an inference with an empty premise list is refused. The reverse is also refused — premises on a fact that was not inferred are meaningless, and quietly accepting them would make the proof tree unreliable. 3. An inference is never more confident than its weakest premise Without this rule, a chain of guesses can launder itself into a certainty: three facts at 0.6 combine into a conclusion at 0.95, and nothing in the record shows what happened. The build function refuses any inference whose confidence exceeds the minimum of its premises. 4. Governing relationships are validated against a closed list at write time The failure this prevents is specific and worth stating concretely. An extractor records is_counsel_to. A conflict check queries REPRESENTS. Zero rows come back. The report reads as a clean conflict check, and it is not one — it is a query that missed a synonym. A write that fails loudly is enormously preferable to a query that silently returns nothing. See The predicate vocabulary. 5. Review state is derived from the class, never accepted from the caller See below. This is the invariant most worth understanding. A sixth rule, enforced elsewhere Retracting a fact must transitively retract every conclusion that rested on it. That cannot live with the other five because they each inspect one candidate assertion in isolation, whereas this one has to walk the graph of premises. It lives in the retraction module instead. Nothing is ever deleted: a retraction marks the fact superseded from a moment in time, so a reading of the graph as it stood before that moment still shows the fact and still shows the conclusion it supported. That is what transaction time is for. Why it matters more than it looks: the failure is silent. Retract the extraction that said counsel represents a party, leave the conflict flag standing, and the graph now asserts a conflict whose stated basis has been withdrawn. Every "why do you believe this?" answer for that flag then cites a retracted premise — which is precisely the question the system exists to answer well. Why review state is derived, not chosen The obvious design is a field that each part of the pipeline sets: a citation parser writes AUTO_ASSERTED, a model extractor writes PENDING. It is also the design that fails, and it fails in the way that is hardest to detect. If review state is an input, then every code path that creates an assertion is a code path that can opt out of review. Not maliciously — by a mistaken default, a copy-pasted call, a new ingest route written in a hurry, a well-intentioned bulk backfill. And the failure is invisible: the graph looks the same, answers look the same, and the only symptom is that some facts nobody approved are shaping results. A code review cannot catch it reliably, because the check is "did the author of this call site think about review?" and the answer is unknowable from the diff. So review state is not a parameter. The function that builds an assertion computes it from the epistemic class and nothing else: DECLARED → AUTO_ASSERTED EXTRACTED_DET → AUTO_ASSERTED EXTRACTED_MODEL → PENDING INFERRED → PENDING PREDICTED → PENDING The two auto-asserted classes are exactly the two that involve no unverified judgement. A catalogue is a system of record. A confirmed quote was confirmed. Neither has anything for a human signature to add, and asking for one would be theatre. Everything else waits. Because the mapping is computed rather than supplied, "no ingest path can opt out of review" is a property of the type, not a convention the team maintains. The application's own wording for this, shown to users as a tooltip, is worth quoting because it is the same claim in plainer words: Whether a person has signed this off. Derived from how the fact was reached, not chosen: a fact declared by a system of record, or a quote the system confirmed is on the page, goes live directly. Anything a model read into a document, and anything inferred, waits for a person. No ingest path can opt out of review. Two gates that are easily confused There are two separate questions about a fact, and conflating them causes real confusion: Review state — has a human signed off on this claim? Derived from the class, as above. Staged or live — is this claim in the part of the graph that queries read? An auto-asserted citation is signed off the moment it is created, but it still has to be written. Keeping them apart is what makes a bad extraction run harmless. Staging is a transaction boundary: a whole document's assertions land together or not at all, so a half-ingested filing never looks like a complete one. A document that failed halfway through extraction contributes nothing rather than contributing a misleading subset. And since the original file is held immutably, re-running costs a re-extraction and nothing else. How this is stored, and why it is denormalised A fact is written in two places at once: (:Matter)-[:ADVERSE_TO {assertion_id, epistemic_class, confidence, review_state, superseded_at, tenant_id, matter_id}]->(:Party) (:Assertion {assertion_id, method, source_locator, valid_from, recorded_at, reviewed_by, ...})-[:PREMISE]->(:Assertion) The relationship itself carries only the small subset a filtered traversal needs, so "walk only the edges I trust" stays a single hop. The full provenance and the premise structure live on a separate node and are read only when somebody asks why. This is deliberately not the textbook answer. Storing every fact purely as a node with relationships pointing at it — full reification — would make every read three times the hops. Storing everything on the relationship's own properties could not express a proof tree at all, because a relationship cannot point at another relationship. The cost of the hybrid is two writes per fact that have to stay consistent with each other, which is a real cost, accepted knowingly. Not built yet The writer that would perform those two writes does not exist. Assertions are currently held in an in-process store and are lost on restart, and the read path reads from that store rather than from the graph database. The schema, the indexes and the scoped-read mechanism are all in place. Note that the in-memory store maintains a reverse index from premise to conclusion, which the retraction cascade walks — whatever replaces it has to maintain the same thing, or cascading retraction breaks silently.

title: How extraction works
summary: Reading facts out of documents is where a system like this either earns its defensibility or quietly loses it. LexGraph has one extraction path — a language model — and splits its output not by who proposed a claim but by whether the claim can be checked.

headings.text: Why EXTRACTED_DET means "a check confirmed it"
Why only MENTIONS may be verified presence
Why the split exists at all
What else gets dropped, and why silently is fine
Text is searchable before any of this is reviewed

body: How it works How extraction works Reading facts out of documents is where a system like this either earns its defensibility or quietly loses it. LexGraph has one extraction path — a language model — and splits its output not by who proposed a claim but by whether the claim can be checked. src/documents/extractors/model.py The shape of it A document arrives, is converted to text with page numbers preserved, and is split into passages. Each passage goes to a language model once, with a system prompt that asks for two kinds of claim and insists on keeping them separate, because they are checked differently: Entities — something named in the passage: a party, a court, an authority, a date, a docket number. This is a claim about presence only. It is verified by searching the passage for the model's quote, so the quote must be copied exactly. Relationships — something the passage supports that no search could confirm: that one holding undercuts another, that a clause supersedes an earlier one, that a party is positioned against another. These go to a human reviewer. Everything the model returns is then put through two gates before anything reaches the graph, both of them there because model output is untrusted input: The relationship name must exist in the vocabulary, matched exactly. An invented name is dropped rather than quietly widening the schema. No model adjudicates whether two names mean the same thing — see The predicate vocabulary. The quote must actually appear in the passage. A claim whose quote cannot be found is dropped entirely, not stored with a caveat. The verifier The check itself is unglamorous, which is the point. The model returns a quote; the code searches the passage text for it. An exact match is preferred. Failing that, the quote is matched allowing any run of whitespace where the quote has a space, because a document converter's line joins legitimately differ from how a model echoes a passage — a sentence broken across two lines in the PDF comes back to the model as one line, and refusing that would reject correct claims for a typesetting reason. Anything beyond whitespace differences is paraphrase, and the claim is dropped. A quote a reader cannot find in the document is not provenance. The application says the same thing to users this way: The words from the document, copied exactly. Not a summary: a paraphrase could not be searched for in the original, so a claim whose quote cannot be found on the stated page is refused rather than recorded. When the check passes, both halves of what happened are recorded in the fact's method field: llm:global.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5+verify:quote@v1 A model proposed it; the quote check confirmed it. The verifier carries its own version number, separate from the model's name, so that if quote matching ever changes the previous generation is superseded rather than mixed in with the new one. Why EXTRACTED_DET means "a check confirmed it" The class name EXTRACTED_DET reads as though it means "extracted deterministically", and in an earlier version of this system it did: a regular expression found a citation and the citation went into the graph. That extractor no longer exists. The class was redefined rather than retired, and the redefinition is the most important idea on this page. The reversal EXTRACTED_DET no longer means "a regex found it". It means a deterministic check confirmed it: a model proposes that some text appears on some page, and a string search against that page either agrees or does not. The proposal is probabilistic; the confirmation is not, and the confirmation is what the class records. That keeps the class meaningful. It now means "a deterministic check confirmed this", rather than "a pattern matched something", and it lets the review queue hold only genuine judgement calls. No allowlist anywhere. The value of this is that the split between "goes live immediately" and "waits for a person" no longer depends on who proposed the claim. It depends on whether the claim is checkable. A model is perfectly capable of producing a claim that a machine can verify, and when it does, a human signature adds nothing. Insisting on one would be theatre, and expensive theatre — see why the split exists at all. Why only MENTIONS may be verified presence A quote match establishes exactly one thing: that these words appear on this page. It establishes nothing about what they mean. So only relationships that claim presence and nothing more may carry the verified class. In the legal vocabulary that is a single relationship, MENTIONS, and the constraint is enforced by the assertion builder rather than left to the extractor's good behaviour. Anything that implies significance stays a model interpretation and waits for review: CITES implies reliance, ADVERSE_TO implies a position, SUPERSEDES implies a legal effect. None of those is established by finding words on a page. This constraint exists because of a specific, real bug in the earlier design. The Brown v. Board example The old citation parser auto-asserted CITES whenever it matched the shape of a case citation. So the sentence The court declined to follow Brown. was recorded in the graph as reliance on Brown — an edge asserting that this document cites that authority, entering the graph with no review, at high confidence, because a pattern had matched. The parser could not read negation. It could not read hypotheticals ("had the plaintiff relied on Brown…"), or a string cite in a passage distinguishing the case, or a reference inside a block quote from the opposing brief. It matched shape, not meaning. Now: the model reads the sentence and proposes something interpretive — that the document distinguishes Brown, say. Nothing can mechanically confirm that reading, so it is EXTRACTED_MODEL , capped below the trust threshold, and waits for a lawyer. Separately, the fact that the words "Brown" appear on that page can be confirmed by search, so a MENTIONS edge is verified and goes live. The document becomes findable immediately; the claim about reliance does not exist until a person agrees with it. The distinction the example turns on is worth stating flatly: finding a name is not the same as recording what the name was doing there. The old design collapsed the two, and the consequence was a graph that asserted reliance that never existed — the exact kind of fact this system would then confidently defend, with a page citation, to somebody who trusted it. Why there are no allowlists The deleted extractor had real virtues. It ran in a third of a millisecond, made no network call, and produced byte-identical output across a hundred runs. Those are not small things, and they did not survive contact with the requirement. Three reasons, and the second is the subtle one: Its offsets pointed into a buffer nobody can see The character offsets it recorded indexed the document converter's reconstructed text buffer, not the PDF. No viewer can seek to them. There was a test proving the offsets were internally consistent, and it proved consistency with a buffer no user will ever open. Worse: re-parsing a document after a converter version change shifts every offset downstream, silently repointing stored assertions at the wrong text. See Provenance. Its allowlists silently missed anything not enumerated It carried a list of roughly forty-five reporter abbreviations and around twenty court name patterns. A court that nobody had thought to enumerate simply did not exist in the graph. No error, no warning, no gap visible anywhere — the document was processed successfully and the court was absent. And then the failure compounded. A separate guard existed to stop the model from proposing relationships the deterministic parser was responsible for, on the sound reasoning that two producers competing for the same relationship would create duplicate and conflicting edges. Put the two rules together and a novel court could not be extracted by the parser and was blocked from being rescued by the model. Two individually defensible rules combining into a dead end, with silence as the symptom. The judgement that resolved it Maintaining allowlists is a cost that has to be paid forever, by somebody who knows which reporters and courts exist, and the failure mode of not paying it is invisible. A strong model is better at exactly the classification the pattern matcher got wrong. So the allowlists went, along with the extractor that needed them, and the prompt deliberately contains no list of known courts or reporters. It auto-asserted a relationship implying reliance Covered above. This was the one that made the decision easy. Why the split exists at all An obvious objection to all of this: if the model is untrusted, why does any of its output go live without review? Why not review everything it says? Because a queue nobody can clear gets rubber-stamped, and a rubber-stamped queue destroys the guarantee it exists to provide. A 300-page bundle produces hundreds of extracted claims. If every one needed a human decision, the queue for a single matter would be unclearable, and the predictable human response is to approve in bulk without reading. At that point the review state on every fact in the system is a lie: it says a person checked this, and no person checked it. The system would still print "approved by" on every edge, and the word would mean nothing. So the split is on checkability, not on who proposed the claim. Claims a machine can confirm are confirmed by a machine. The queue holds only genuine judgement calls — the ones where a human actually has something to contribute — and stays small enough that reading it is realistic. Reviewing claims follows this through. The confidence ceiling One more guard, and it is independent of everything above. A model's self-reported confidence is not evidence, so it is capped: an interpretive claim can carry at most 0.79, whatever the model says about itself. The retrieval trust threshold is 0.80. The gap is deliberate and it is load-bearing. An unreviewed model interpretation sits below the threshold by construction, so it cannot shape an answer even if the review gate were bypassed entirely — by a bug, by a misconfigured route, by a future code path nobody has written yet. Two independent mechanisms have to fail before an unapproved interpretation reaches a user. The coupling is enforced in code rather than merely documented; see the cap/floor invariant. A verified presence claim is set to 0.95 rather than 1.0, which is a small point worth making because it is honest. The search proved the words are there. It did not prove that the model normalised those words to the right entity — deciding that "Acme Corp." and the "Acme Corporation" already in the graph are the same company is still the model's work, and it can be wrong. What else gets dropped, and why silently is fine A relationship name that is not in the vocabulary. Logged and discarded. Accepting it would let a model widen the schema. A quote that is not verbatim. Logged and discarded, whether the claim was presence or interpretation. Storing an interpretation with an unverifiable quote would produce a review-queue item a reviewer cannot check. A claim whose subject and object are the same entity. Discarded — a self-referential edge is a normalisation artefact, not a fact. Any claim that violates an assertion contract invariant. Logged and discarded, which is how the presence-predicate constraint is actually enforced: the extractor does not have to remember it, because the builder refuses. A failure anywhere in a document aborts the whole extraction pass rather than staging a partial result. A document half-extracted must not look fully extracted, and the original bytes are still held, so re-running costs one re-extraction and nothing else. Text is searchable before any of this is reviewed Passages are indexed for search before the review gate, deliberately. Verbatim text is a quote, not a claim: putting the words of a document into a search index does not assert anything about what they mean. Lawyers expect to be able to search a document the moment it lands, and withholding that for hours while a queue is worked would make the product unusable. The review gate protects the graph — the structured claims that shape answers — not the search index. A stricter posture is defensible and was considered; it was rejected as unusable rather than overlooked.

title: Provenance
summary: A citation is only worth having if somebody can check it. That single test decided the shape of provenance in this system, and it overturned the design that came first.

Why presigned URLs are never stored
The original file is the only source of truth

body: How it works Provenance A citation is only worth having if somebody can check it. That single test decided the shape of provenance in this system, and it overturned the design that came first. src/graph/assertions.py (SourceLocator) · src/documents/storage.py The test a citation has to pass Ask what a lawyer actually does when they want to verify a claim about a document. They open the file, turn to the page, and look for the sentence. That is the whole procedure, it works with any viewer, and it has worked for as long as there have been documents. So provenance for a fact read from a document is three things: the file — which document, by identity, plus its original filename for display the page — the page the passage came from, carried through conversion and splitting the quote — the words themselves, copied exactly Nothing else is required, and nothing else is trusted. The application phrases it this way to users: The citation for a fact read from a document: the file, the page, and the words themselves. It is deliberately what you would use to check it by hand — open the file at that page and search for the sentence. Any viewer can do that, and it still works after the document is re-processed. The quote is load-bearing rather than decorative. It is what a document viewer searches for, what a reviewer reads when deciding whether to approve a claim, and what a fingerprint is taken over so that a later change to the underlying document becomes detectable. A document citation without a quote is refused at construction — the object cannot be created. A citation with nothing to search for cannot be checked, which defeats the point of recording it. Why character offsets were demoted The first design made character offsets the primary mechanism: a fact pointed at characters 1,240 to 1,318 of a document. This is precise, it is easy to compute, and it is a false precision. It was reversed, and the reasoning is the useful part. The reversal Character offsets index the document converter's reconstructed text buffer, not the PDF. (The converter is Amazon Textract, which returns text plus layout and page numbers.) There are two problems with that, and each is sufficient on its own. No viewer can seek to them. The buffer is an intermediate artefact produced during conversion. It is not the file the user opens, and there is no mapping from a position in it to a position on a rendered page. A citation that points into it is only checkable by a program that reproduces the same conversion — which is to say, only by the system making the claim. That is not provenance; it is the system citing itself. Re-parsing shifts them. When the document conversion service changes version, its reconstruction of the same PDF changes slightly — a header handled differently, a table serialised in another order, whitespace normalised in a new way — and every offset after that point moves. Nothing errors. Stored assertions silently now point at different text than they did. A citation that was correct on Tuesday quotes a different sentence on Wednesday, and there is no signal anywhere that it happened. There was a test asserting the offsets were internally consistent. It passed. It was verifying consistency with a buffer nobody can see. Offsets are still recorded, as optional diagnostic metadata, and they are useful for debugging a chunking problem. They are never the citation. The application labels them for users so nobody mistakes them for one: An internal position within the extracted text, kept only for diagnosis. It does not correspond to a position in the file you would open, so it is not the citation — the file, page and quote are. Safe to ignore. File, page and quote survive re-parsing. If the converter changes and the page a sentence lands on is unchanged, the citation still resolves. If a page number did change, the quote still finds it. The mechanism degrades gracefully; offsets fail silently. That is the whole argument. The fingerprint Alongside the quote, a hash of the quoted text is stored when the fact is recorded. Its purpose is narrow and worth stating: it detects the case where the underlying document has been replaced. If the words at the cited location no longer hash to the recorded value, the fact is flagged rather than left to drift. In the application's words: A fingerprint of the quoted words taken when the fact was recorded. If the underlying document is ever replaced, the fingerprint stops matching and the fact is flagged rather than silently drifting. Provenance for facts from databases Facts that come from structured sources — the data catalogue, a table of invoices — carry a different locator: the source, the table, the column, and a hash of the query that produced the result. The same requirement applies: it must be possible to go back to where the number came from and get the same number. Structured sources never move their data into LexGraph. Only metadata about them — tables, columns, metric definitions — enters the graph. The rows themselves are queried in place at the moment a question is asked. A locator therefore describes a repeatable query, not a copy. Why presigned URLs are never stored Documents live in object storage that is not publicly readable. To let a user open one, the system mints a presigned URL: a link that carries its own temporary authorisation and expires. It is tempting to store that link on the fact, so that "check this citation" is a stored hyperlink. Two reasons not to, and they point in opposite directions. An expiring credential is provenance that stops resolving A presigned URL is valid for minutes. An audit trail whose citations are dead links a week later is worse than useless, because the failure looks like the fact being wrong rather than the link having expired. Provenance has to resolve when someone asks in two years, in a dispute, about a document nobody has opened since. A stored URL is a bearer credential sitting in a database Once a presigned URL exists, it answers to nobody. It carries its own authorisation, so it works for whoever holds it, regardless of who they are, whether they are logged in, or whether they were ever entitled to the document. It bypasses every application-level check by design. Writing one into a record is putting a working key to a client's file into a row that will be backed up, replicated, and read by processes that have no idea what it is. What is done instead The fact stores the document's identity. A link is minted at the moment somebody clicks, and only after that caller's access to the document's matter has been checked — because once the URL exists, no later check can stop it. The storage layer adds its own tenant check as a second line of defence, which is cheap and catches a wrong document identifier before it becomes a credential. Links default to 15 minutes and are hard-capped at one hour. Beyond that a link stops being a click-through and becomes an unrevocable, unauditable copy of the document. The cap is enforced, not advisory. Two small details in the same code are there for the reviewer's benefit rather than for security. The link asks the browser to display the file inline rather than download it, because a reviewer is checking a citation, not collecting a file. And if the fact cites a page, the page number is appended as a URL fragment — fragments are never sent to the server, so this does not disturb the link's signature, and every PDF viewer honours it. The reviewer lands on the cited page. The original file is the only source of truth Uploaded bytes go to immutable, versioned, encrypted object storage, and everything else — the graph, the search index — is a derived index that can be dropped and rebuilt from it. This has one consequence that matters more than it sounds: a bad extraction run is never a data-loss event. If an extractor is wrong, if a model behaves badly, if a whole ingest pass produces nonsense, the remedy is to discard the derived facts and run again. The evidence is untouched. That is what makes it reasonable to change extraction logic at all, which is in turn what made it possible to delete the pattern-matching extractor rather than living with it. Keys in storage are content-addressed under a per-firm prefix. The prefix is not decoration: a storage policy can pin a role to one firm's prefix, so a bug that computes the wrong key fails at the storage permission boundary instead of reading another firm's file. Content addressing also makes a double upload idempotent — the same bytes produce the same key, and the second upload is skipped rather than creating a second version that a retention policy would then forbid deleting. Deleting a document writes a deletion marker rather than destroying bytes, and object lock means a genuine erasure requires a privileged bypass. That shape is intentional: routine deletes are recoverable, and an actual erasure request is a deliberate, audited act rather than a click. Provenance for derived facts A fact that a rule worked out has no page to cite, because no document says it. Its provenance is its premises — the facts it was derived from — and following those down produces a proof tree that terminates in documents and records. The full chain of reasoning behind an inferred fact, unwound to the documents and records at its base. If any step in it is wrong, the conclusion is wrong, and you can see which step. Two contract rules make this trustworthy rather than decorative. A derived fact with no premises cannot be created at all. And a derived fact can never be more confident than the weakest fact it rests on, so a chain of uncertain steps cannot present itself as a certainty. Not built yet No reasoning engine fires the rules, so no derived facts currently exist. The premise structure, the confidence ceiling, the retraction cascade that walks premises, and the interface for reading a proof tree are all built and tested. Two rules are written out in the legal vocabulary pack. There is nothing to execute them.

title: Tenancy and ethical walls
summary: Two firms' data sits in one database, separated by a filter. That is an uncomfortable sentence, and the honest version of it raised the stakes on one file until it was built to a standard that matches.

headings.text: Why not a separate graph per matter?
The correction: there is no structural isolation
What that one module does about it
Why a denial always beats a permission
Why a walled matter answers 404 and not 403
The one thing a walled user is told
Automated callers have no identity of their own

body: How it works Tenancy and ethical walls Two firms' data sits in one database, separated by a filter. That is an uncomfortable sentence, and the honest version of it raised the stakes on one file until it was built to a standard that matches. src/graph/scope.py · src/graph/client.py · src/api/app.py Two levels of isolation A tenant is one firm. A matter is one engagement — a case, a transaction, an advisory instruction — inside a firm. Both are enforced as filters on every read, and they differ in exactly one respect: who is allowed to change them. Level Set by Changes Tenant Fixed at authentication, read from the verified sign-in token. Never from a request parameter — a caller who could name their own tenant could widen their own access. Effectively never. Matter The caller's authorisation grants: a list of matters they may see, and a list they may not. Weekly, as staffing changes. The matter level changing weekly is why it must be policy rather than data layout. An ethical wall goes up when a lawyer is staffed onto a matter that conflicts with one they have been working on, and it has to take effect immediately. If isolation were a property of where data lived, raising a wall would be a data migration, and nobody raises a wall that takes a migration. Why not a separate graph per matter? Because conflict checking is, by definition, across matters — and the shared entity is the signal. If Acme Corp appears in forty matters, that is one node with forty relationships attached. A query asking "does the firm both represent and oppose this company?" is a short walk around that node. Split the graph per matter and Acme Corp becomes forty unconnected nodes, the walk is impossible, and the conflict check has to be rebuilt as a search-and-compare across databases — which is the thing knowledge graphs are good at, given up for an isolation model that was not needed. The correction: there is no structural isolation An earlier version of this design claimed tenants were isolated structurally, each in its own named graph, and said so in the project's own README. It was wrong. The reversal Named graphs are a concept from RDF and SPARQL, a different family of graph technology. The graph database in use here — Neptune Database — holds one property graph per cluster, and the query language it speaks, openCypher, has no notion of a named graph at all. There was nothing to isolate structurally. The claim described a feature of a different product. So tenant and matter isolation are both property filters, differing only in who may change them. This was corrected in the code and in that module's own documentation rather than quietly patched, because the honest version raises the stakes on that one module: it is now the only thing standing between two firms' data, and it should be read knowing that. A related option was examined and rejected. Neptune Analytics, a sibling product, does have discrete graph resources, so a graph per tenant is expressible there. But each one provisions a minimum of around 32 GB of capacity with no automatic scaling, which makes it a per-customer deployment shape rather than multi-tenant software. It also speaks only openCypher and has no full-text search. The considered conclusion is that a graph per tenant is affordable only if each tenant is a deployment, and that is a different business. What that one module does about it The design rule the scoping module exists to enforce is stated in the code as: it must be impossible to express an unscoped query. Not discouraged. Not reviewed for. Impossible. One forgotten tenant filter in one code path is a cross-firm privilege breach, and a privilege breach is not a bug that gets patched and moved past. Three mechanisms, layered: No part of the system outside the graph package writes a graph query by hand. Callers describe the shape of the traversal they want; the scoping module owns the filter clause. The metric compiler, for instance, reads a schema interface rather than the graph client, partly for this reason — and gained the side benefit that its tests need no database. The client refuses to run a read that has not been scoped. A read must contain a placeholder token where the scoping clause belongs; a query without it is rejected before it reaches the database. Interpolating anything else is not offered. There is no argument anywhere meaning "skip scoping". The narrow query object the scoping module returns can be narrowed further by a caller but has no operation that widens it. Every scoped read composes five independent filters, each of which was a deliberate decision and so is named explicitly rather than buried in a query string: Tenant — the firm, from the verified token. Matter walls — the allowlist, then the denylist. Trust classes — which kinds of belief may inform an answer. Guesses are excluded here, and excluded a second time even if a caller passes them in explicitly. Confidence threshold — facts below the floor are visible in the review queue but do not shape answers. Time — by default only facts believed now; optionally, what was believed on a given date. That last one is how "what did the file show when we advised?" is answered. Asking as of a past date returns facts that were believed then, including ones since retracted, because the question is about what was known at the time and not about what is true now. Why a denial always beats a permission A user's matter access is two lists: an allowlist of matters they may see, and a denylist of matters they may not. The denylist is applied after the allowlist and always wins. The reason is that ethical walls and broad roles coexist, and they coexist in exactly the configuration where getting this wrong is worst. A senior partner has firm-wide access as a matter of role. That same partner is walled off from one matter because they previously acted for the other side. If a permission could satisfy a request that a wall forbids, then the broadest role in the firm defeats every wall in the firm — and the people with the broadest roles are precisely the people most likely to have a conflicting history. So the wall wins. This mirrors the underlying authorisation language, where a forbid overrides any permit, and it means a wall cannot be defeated by also holding a broad role. The application says it to users this way: An ethical wall. Matters you are walled off from are invisible to you: they do not appear in results, counts, or the graph. A denial always beats a permission, so a broad role cannot defeat a wall. Why a walled matter answers 404 and not 403 This is a small technical decision with a large consequence, and it is the one most likely to look like a bug to somebody who has not been told. When a user requests something they are not permitted to see, the conventional response is 403 Forbidden: this exists, and you may not have it. LexGraph returns 404 Not Found: there is no such thing here. Why the conventional answer leaks A 403 confirms existence. And confirming existence is exactly what an ethical wall is meant to prevent. Consider a lawyer walled off from the firm's work for a company they used to act against. If probing a matter identifier returns 403, they learn the matter exists. Probe a list of plausible identifiers, or client names, and the 403 responses map out the firm's engagements — which is material non-public information about who the firm acts for, obtainable by a user who was specifically walled off from learning it. No document was read. The error codes were enough. So the refusal is deliberately vague, and it is vague consistently. The scoping layer's own error message does not distinguish "walled off" from "does not exist". The review queue's lookup does not distinguish them. The document store's lookup does not distinguish them. The web layer maps every scope violation to 404 in one place rather than leaving each route to remember. A vagueness that holds in four places out of five is not vagueness; the fifth place is the whole answer. The one thing a walled user is told There is a tension here, and resolving it correctly is the most interesting part of the model. Perfect vagueness would mean a walled user's results are silently narrower than they believe. And silent filtering is a more dangerous failure than the one the wall prevents. A lawyer who runs a conflict check and sees "no conflicts found" concludes there are no conflicts. If the truth was "no conflicts that you can see", the wall has caused precisely the harm it was built to prevent — the firm proceeds on a clean conflict report that was never clean. The resolution is that the two questions are different questions: "Does matter X exist?" — asked by probing a specific identifier. Refused without distinction. Answering it lets a user enumerate what they are walled off from. "Is my view of this complete?" — asked implicitly by every user, all the time. Answered honestly with an aggregate: 3 matters withheld by an ethical wall. No names, no identifiers, nothing that narrows down which. Enough for the lawyer to know their result is partial and to escalate rather than rely on it. A count is not a leak. Knowing that three matters are withheld tells a user nothing about which three, and it prevents them drawing a false conclusion from an incomplete answer. Known gap to close The interface currently derives that count on the client side from a flag on each matter, which would require the server to send walled matter objects to a user who may not see them — precisely what the model forbids. The endpoint must return visible matters plus a withheld count, never the walled objects even flagged as such. This is recorded as a required change in the project's own API contract; it is not yet made. Automated callers have no identity of their own LexGraph exposes its capabilities to AI agents as tools. Those tools carry no service identity and no standalone credentials. Every call carries the acting user's delegated token and is authorised as that user, with that user's walls. This is non-negotiable where privilege is involved. An agent with its own broad credentials is a path around every ethical wall in the firm, and it is a path that leaves no trace of whose question it was answering. The tool surface runs the same code as the web interface — the same scoping module, the same vocabulary gate — for a related reason: a tool that answered a question differently from the equivalent web request would mean two implementations of governance, and the tool one is the one nobody audits. The seam for physical separation Some customers will eventually require their data to be physically separate rather than logically separated. The scoping module anticipates it with a single function that returns a storage key for a tenant. Today that key is used for naming resources — storage prefixes, search index names. If a contract ever requires a separate database cluster per firm, it becomes the cluster selector, and no calling code changes. This is cheap to have now because every read already carries tenant identity through one place. It would be close to impossible to add later if those filters were scattered across hundreds of call sites, which is the argument for the discipline in the first place.

title: The predicate vocabulary
summary: A predicate is the middle of a fact: the relationship in "counsel represents party". LexGraph keeps two vocabularies of them, one closed and one open, and the test for which list a relationship belongs in is a single question about consequences.

headings.text: The failure the closed list prevents
Why grounding uses no language model
Rules live in the pack too

body: How it works The predicate vocabulary A predicate is the middle of a fact: the relationship in "counsel represents party". LexGraph keeps two vocabularies of them, one closed and one open, and the test for which list a relationship belongs in is a single question about consequences. src/ontology/loader.py · ontologies/legal.yaml Two tiers Every fact in the graph is three parts: a subject, a predicate, an object. Counsel Smith — represents — Acme Corp. The predicate is the relationship name, and how strictly it is controlled turns out to matter a great deal. Governing predicates Closed list. Fourteen of them in the legal pack. These drive decisions with legal consequence: conflicts, privilege, deadlines, citation authority. A fact using a name outside the list is rejected when written. Descriptive predicates Open list. Subject-matter tags: what a document is about, what industry a party is in, what kind of deal something is. Sprawl here costs search precision, not a negligence claim. The test for which tier a relationship belongs in, stated in the vocabulary file itself: Would a wrong answer here embarrass you, or expose you? Embarrass → descriptive. Expose → governing. The legal pack's governing list covers REPRESENTS, ADVERSE_TO, PARTY_TO, CITES, OVERRULES, DISTINGUISHES, FILED_IN, DEADLINE_FOR, SUBJECT_TO_PRIVILEGE, SUPERSEDES, GOVERNED_BY, CONTAINS_CLAUSE, RELATES_TO_MATTER and INSTRUCTS. Its descriptive list is CONCERNS_TOPIC, IN_INDUSTRY, HAS_DEAL_TYPE and MENTIONS. A relationship name the vocabulary has never seen at all is treated as descriptive. That asymmetry is intentional: a new subject-matter tag should not require a vocabulary release, whereas a new governing relationship is a deliberate schema decision that somebody should have to make on purpose. The failure the closed list prevents This is not a data-quality annoyance. It is the single most instructive failure in the system, because the symptom is a clean-looking report. The conflict check that returns nothing An extractor reads a document and records that a firm acts for a company. It names the relationship is_counsel_to — a reasonable name, produced by a model that was not told otherwise, or by a developer who did not check. Later, a conflict check runs. It asks the graph: who do we represent? It queries REPRESENTS. Zero rows come back. Now look at what that means from the outside. The check ran. It did not error. It returned a result. The result was empty. Every signal available to the person reading the report says the same thing an actually-clean conflict check would say: no conflicts found. The firm proceeds. The conflict exists, is recorded in the graph, and was invisible to the query that was written to find it — because of a synonym. This is not a bug that produces a wrong number. It is a bug that produces a reassuring number, and it is why the check is at write time. The design conclusion follows directly: a write that fails loudly is enormously preferable to a query that silently returns nothing. So a governing relationship name is validated against the closed list at the moment a fact is created, and an unapproved name is refused with an error that explains what to do — map it to an approved relationship, or classify it as descriptive. The same reasoning is why the descriptive list is open. If a document is tagged concerns_topic: shipping by one extractor and about_subject: shipping by another, search precision suffers. Somebody finds fewer relevant documents than they might have. That is a bad day. It is not a malpractice event, and paying the cost of a closed list — a vocabulary release for every new tag — to prevent it would be paying the wrong price. Why grounding uses no language model Grounding is the step that maps a proposed relationship name onto one the vocabulary knows. When a model returns acts_on_behalf_of, something has to decide whether that means REPRESENTS. In LexGraph that decision is made by exact matching and nothing else. The proposed name is normalised — trimmed, upper-cased, spaces and hyphens turned into underscores — and compared against the vocabulary's identifiers and their display labels. A match returns the canonical name. No match returns nothing, and the claim is dropped. So represents, REPRESENTS, Represents and adverse to all ground successfully. acts_on_behalf_of does not, and is discarded. The rejected alternative A more permissive mode exists in a comparable system: a language model adjudicates whether two relationship names mean the same thing, and maps the proposal onto the vocabulary accordingly. It would raise recall noticeably, and it was rejected. The reason is that a model deciding acts_on_behalf_of means REPRESENTS is a schema decision made by a model. Schema decisions in a system that must be defensible belong to people, in a versioned file, reviewable by whoever will have to answer for them. A model that gets it right nine times in ten is a model that has silently redefined a governing relationship one time in ten, and there is no record of it having happened. Losing recall to strictness is a visible cost — a claim was dropped, and the log says so. Gaining recall by letting a model edit the schema is an invisible cost. Between a visible cost and an invisible one, in this system, the visible one wins every time. The consequence of strictness is that dropping claims is normal and expected. A model proposing an unrecognised relationship has its claim discarded and logged. That is the system working: no model output silently widens the vocabulary. Vocabulary packs and domain-independence The vocabulary lives in a file, not in code. A pack names the entity types of a domain, its two tiers of relationships, and its rules. The platform loads whichever pack it is pointed at, and the legal pack is simply the default. A second pack for healthcare ships alongside it. Not because healthcare is a target market, but because a claim to be domain-agnostic that has only ever been tested against one domain is a claim that will fail the first time it is tested. If the second pack ever stops loading cleanly, the abstraction has rotted, and it is much better to learn that from a test than from a customer. The healthcare pack applies the same two-tier test, with "expose" reinterpreted for the domain: there, it means patient harm or a regulatory finding, so contraindications and consent are governing. The entity types map recognisably onto the legal ones — a patient plays the role a party does, an encounter plays the role a matter does — which is a good sign that the abstraction is real rather than a legal model with the labels changed. Rules live in the pack too A pack can define rules that derive new facts from existing ones. Each rule names the pattern it fires on, the fact it produces, its own version, and — importantly — the minimum kind of belief its premises must have. The legal pack defines two: Rule Fires when Produces conflict_check The firm represents a party, and a matter is adverse to that same party. A potential-conflict flag on that matter. authority_stale A document cites an authority, and another authority overrules it. A flag that the document relies on stale authority. Both require premises at least as solid as a confirmed extraction. The pack states why for the conflict check, and the reasoning generalises: a conflict flag resting on a language model's guess would be worse than none. Worse, not merely less useful — because a false conflict flag consumes senior time, may cause a firm to decline profitable work, and erodes trust in every other flag the system raises. The rule declines to fire rather than fire on a guess. Not built yet Nothing executes these rules. They are parsed, exposed through the interface, and carry a correctly-formed method string for the facts they would produce. No engine fires them, so no derived facts exist. The premise structure and the confidence ceiling that would constrain them are built and tested. Two other fields in the pack are similarly read but not yet acted on: a relationship can be marked symmetric, and a rule declares a minimum premise class. Both are parsed and shown through the interface; neither is enforced anywhere, because the component that would enforce them is the reasoning engine. The safe default When an extractor sees two entities in the same passage but cannot justify anything stronger, the right answer is MENTIONS — a descriptive relationship recording that a name appears in the text, with no claim about what it was doing there. This is the relationship a verified quote produces, and the only one it may produce. It is also the deliberate answer to a case where a stronger relationship looks free and is not: a case caption reading "Acme Corp v. Beta Holdings" proves both names appear. It does not establish, by mechanical means, that Acme is adverse to Beta — reading adversity out of a caption is interpretation, and interpretation disqualifies a claim from being treated as mechanically confirmed. The consequence is honest and worth naming: adverse-party relationships do not come free from captions. If they are wanted, they belong to the model extractor with review, or to a rule with premises. That is a cost, and it is the correct cost. See How extraction works for the citation-parsing version of the same mistake, which is the one that actually shipped before being reversed.

title: Asking questions
summary: A question is tried against four routes, most precise first. Which route answered is part of the answer, because "this came from an approved definition" and "a model wrote this query" are different claims about how much the number can be trusted.

headings.text: Why tier 2 is the differentiating one
What comes back with an answer

body: Using it Asking questions A question is tried against four routes, most precise first. Which route answered is part of the answer, because "this came from an approved definition" and "a model wrote this query" are different claims about how much the number can be trusted. src/query/resolver.py The four tiers Each route is attempted in turn and declines if it cannot answer. The first one that can, does, and reports itself. 1 Governed metric An approved metric definition matched the question, and that definition compiled to SQL. Trust: the highest available. No model wrote any part of the query. The same question produces the same SQL every time, so the same question produces the same answer. 2 Graph traversal The answer came from walking assertions in the graph — only those above the confidence threshold, approved where approval was required, and visible to this user. Trust: every fact in the answer is a cited assertion that can be opened to a page or a proof tree. A model may phrase the prose; it does not supply the facts. 3 Hybrid Relevant passages are retrieved by similarity, then the graph is expanded outward from the documents they came from, following only trusted relationships. Trust: sources are cited, and the expansion cannot pull in facts that fail the trust filters. Less precise than tier 2 because similarity search decides what to look at. 4 Generated SQL No approved definition matched, so a model writes SQL against the real schema. It is checked against a query firewall before it runs. Trust: not a governed answer. Treat it as a starting point, read the SQL, and check it before relying on the number. This is the only tier an administrator can switch off. If all four decline, the answer says so plainly rather than producing something: no approved metric matched and nothing relevant was found in the graph. Rephrasing may help, or the question may need a metric definition that does not exist yet. An empty answer that admits it is empty is worth considerably more than a plausible one. Why tier 2 is the differentiating one Tier 1 is a good idea that other systems have. Tier 3, in isolation, is what most document AI does: find similar passages, hand them to a model, get prose back. Tier 2 is different in kind. It expands along assertions rather than along similarity. A question like "which matters involve Acme Corporation" is answered by finding the Acme entity and walking the relationships attached to it — where every relationship walked has a class, a confidence, a method, and a page citation, and where relationships that fail the trust filters are not walked at all. The practical difference shows up in what comes back with the answer. Every resolution carries a list of the assertions it used. That list is what makes the answer auditable rather than merely labelled: each identifier in it resolves to a document span or a proof tree. A retrieval system can tell you which passages it looked at. This can tell you which facts it relied on, and let you reject any one of them. Matching in tier 2 is lexical — entity names and relationship names, not embeddings. That is deliberate rather than a shortcut: a question naming Acme Corporation should find the Acme entity by name, and doing it lexically means the result is reproducible and the reason for it is explainable. The system reports which terms matched, so the interface can explain why a fact was included. Semantics enter at tier 3, where they are labelled as such. The kill switch Tier 4 can be switched off per firm. When it is, a question that reaches it is refused rather than answered: This question could not be answered from an approved metric or the knowledge graph, and ungoverned queries are switched off. An administrator can review blocked questions in Governance. The reason only tier 4 has a switch is that it is the only tier where the system is guessing at intent rather than executing something a person approved. Tiers 1 through 3 execute definitions, traversals and retrievals that a human designed. Tier 4 asks a model to invent a query, and the model's understanding of the question is the only thing standing between the user and a wrong number that looks right. Some firms will accept that trade for the coverage. Some will not, particularly during onboarding or in a regulated practice area. The switch makes that a policy choice rather than a product choice, and the application explains it to administrators this way: Refuses any question that no approved governed metric can answer, rather than falling back to model-generated SQL. Governed metrics keep working. Refused questions are logged and make a good backlog of metrics worth defining. The refusal log is a backlog Refused questions are recorded — the firm, the user, the question, the reason, the time — and shown to administrators. This is not an audit trail for its own sake. A question people keep asking is a governed metric waiting to be written. That reframes the switch from a restriction into a product feedback loop. Turn it on, watch what gets refused, and the list of definitions worth building writes itself in the users' own words. The query firewall When tier 4 does run, the SQL a model produces is checked before it is executed. The check parses the query into a syntax tree and walks it, extracting every table referenced anywhere — including inside joins, common table expressions, subqueries and unions — and validates them against what the caller may read. Two properties are worth calling out, because a simpler check misses both: It fails closed on a parse error. A query that cannot be understood is refused, not allowed through on the grounds that nothing suspicious was found. It rejects anything that is not a single read. A comparable implementation checked only table names, which means DELETE FROM allowed_table would have passed — the table was allowed, and nothing looked at the verb. Non-read statements and multiple stacked statements are both refused. Not built yet Tier 4 has no SQL generator wired up, so in practice it always declines. The firewall exists and is tested; the model-backed generator that would feed it does not. The kill switch, however, is fully wired and does refuse — so a firm that turns it on gets the refusal and the audit entry today. What makes a metric governed A governed metric is a definition in a file that compiles to SQL deterministically. It is not a saved query and not a prompt. The fields that carry governance weight, rather than merely describing the number: Field What it governs Time grains The only time buckets this metric may be reported in. Asking for a grain outside the list fails compilation rather than quietly answering at the wrong one. Time grain column The single column those grains govern. Grouping by any other time-like column is refused as a bypass. Additivity Whether the measure may be summed across periods. Fees billed may; a headcount may not, and summing it produces a number that means nothing. Parameters The closed set of columns a caller may filter on. Two of the compiler's governance rules are hard refusals rather than warnings: summing a semi-additive measure across a time grain, and slicing by time on a column the metric does not govern. Both produce a number that looks fine and is wrong, which is the category this system treats most severely. A metric can also be compiled without being executed. That is not a debugging convenience — it is the point of a governed metric. A reviewer can read exactly what a definition will do before approving it. Not built yet Tier 1 returns the compiled SQL with no result attached. The Athena executor is written and tested, with the firewall check inside it, but nothing connects it to the metric path — so the SQL a governed metric compiles to is never run. Requesting the SQL without running it is the honest mode until that wire exists. A composition bug worth recording Metrics can be defined in terms of other metrics. Doing that naively caused a real, subtle error in the system this compiler was modelled on. Comparing one month's billings to another month's time A realisation rate is fees billed divided by the standard value of the time recorded. Two component metrics, combined. The reference implementation joined the two components on their shared dimension names. But the two components measure time on different columns — billings are dated by invoice date, time entries by the date the work was done. There is no shared name to align on. The join produced a number, and the number compared one month's billings against a different month's recorded time. Nothing errored. The rate was plausible. It was wrong in a way that would require somebody to reconcile it by hand to notice. The fix is that every component buckets its time into a shared alias, so the two halves are explicitly aligned on the same period rather than implicitly on a name collision. Composition is also limited to one level deep, on the grounds that a reviewer must be able to read the emitted SQL and follow it. A definition three levels deep compiles to something nobody will check, and an unchecked governed metric is a governed metric in name only. What comes back with an answer Every resolution carries: the tier that answered, and whether it counts as governed a plain-language explanation of what that tier means, written for a lawyer the SQL, where SQL was involved, in full citations — document, page — where documents were involved the assertions used, each of which can be opened to its provenance the tiers attempted, so a tier-3 answer visibly shows that tiers 1 and 2 declined warnings, including the explicit one attached to every tier-4 answer The tier list being visible matters more than it looks. A user who sees that the governed route was tried and declined knows something useful: the question is not one the firm has defined an approved answer for. That is a fact about the firm's own governance, surfaced for free by the answer.

title: Reviewing claims
summary: The review queue is the most important screen in the product, and its most important property is that it is short. A queue nobody can clear gets rubber-stamped, and a rubber-stamped queue destroys the guarantee it exists to provide.

headings.text: Rejecting, and why the reason is mandatory
Staged and live are not the same as reviewed

body: Using it Reviewing claims The review queue is the most important screen in the product, and its most important property is that it is short. A queue nobody can clear gets rubber-stamped, and a rubber-stamped queue destroys the guarantee it exists to provide. src/documents/review.py · src/documents/retract.py What is in the queue Only claims where a human has something to contribute. In practice that means claims whose class is EXTRACTED_MODEL : things a model read into a document rather than merely found in it. Not in the queue: facts a system of record declared, and quotes a search confirmed are on the page. Neither involves an unverified judgement, so there is nothing for a signature to add. Asking for one would produce a record saying a person checked something they did not meaningfully check. The distinction is drawn on checkability, not on who proposed a claim — which is why a model's output can appear on both sides of it. See How extraction works. Why it must stay small This is the argument that shaped the extraction design, and it is worth following because the naive alternative sounds stricter and is in fact weaker.
