Suppose every model output required review. A 300-page bundle produces hundreds of extracted claims. A single matter's ingest would produce a queue of that size, and several matters would produce a queue nobody could work through in a week. What happens then is predictable and human: somebody selects all and approves. Not out of negligence — out of the reasonable judgement that the queue is an obstacle rather than a control, because a control you cannot exercise is an obstacle. And at that moment every review record in the system becomes false. Each fact says a person approved it and names them. No person read it. The system will now print "approved by" alongside facts nobody looked at, and it will do so with complete confidence, to somebody relying on it. The load-bearing claim A review queue's value is not proportional to how much it contains. It is proportional to how much of it gets read. A queue holding ten genuine judgement calls, all read, is worth immeasurably more than a queue holding four hundred claims, bulk-approved — because the second one produces a false audit trail, and a false audit trail is worse than no audit trail. So the queue holds judgement calls and nothing else. Everything mechanically checkable is checked mechanically, and the human is spent where a human is actually required. What a reviewer sees Each row carries what is needed to decide, and no more: the claim itself as subject, relationship and object; how it was reached and by which specific versioned producer; its confidence; the document and page; the quoted sentence; the matter; and when it was recorded. Two ordering choices are worth explaining. Sorted by confidence ascending. The claims the model was least sure of come first, because that is where a reviewer's attention is worth most. Sorting the other way would spend the scarcest resource in the system on the easiest decisions. Retracted claims are excluded. A retraction cascade can withdraw a claim that was still sitting in the queue — the premise it rested on was retracted while it waited. Asking somebody to adjudicate something already withdrawn wastes their time, and worse, approving it would revive a withdrawn fact. Both the listing and the approve path filter on whether a claim is still current. A bug the tests caught Earlier, retracted assertions stayed in the queue and could be approved. The sequence: a cascade retracts a still-pending claim, a reviewer works through the queue, and approving it brings a withdrawn fact back into the live graph — with a fresh approval record attached, making it look more trustworthy than the facts around it. Both paths now check that a claim is current before acting. What approving actually means Approval is a named human act. The reviewer's identity is recorded, mandatory, along with the time and an optional note. There is deliberately no bulk-approve-everything operation in the system: a loop over the queue is one line of caller code, and at least it is a line somebody wrote on purpose. Several transitions are refused, and each refusal is a design statement: Attempt Result Why Approve something already approved Accepted, unchanged Idempotent. A double-click is not an error. Approve something rejected Refused Re-extract rather than reviving a rejected claim, so the audit trail stays honest about what happened. Approve something auto-asserted Refused It needs no approval, and approving it would imply a human checked something they did not. Approve something retracted Refused Its basis was withdrawn. Approving would revive a withdrawn fact. Reject something already live Refused Use retraction instead, so anything inferred from it is invalidated too. The third row is the most unusual and the most characteristic. A system that let you approve auto-asserted facts would let a well-meaning administrator work through the whole graph adding signatures, and the signatures would mean nothing. Refusing the operation keeps the word "approved" meaning one specific thing. Rejecting, and why the reason is mandatory A rejection requires a reason. It is not bookkeeping: the reason is the training signal. It is the only place in the system where a human records why a model was wrong about a document, and that record is what makes it possible to improve extraction rather than merely filter it. Rejected claims are never deleted. A rejected extraction is evidence about the extractor — that a particular version of a particular model, on a particular kind of passage, produced a claim a lawyer disagreed with. Deleting it discards the only data anybody has about how well extraction is working. Staged and live are not the same as reviewed Two questions are easy to conflate, and the difference matters when something goes wrong: Review state — has a person signed this off? Derived from how the fact was reached, and no code path can opt out. Staged or live — is this fact in the part of the graph queries read? A confirmed quote is signed off the moment it is created, but it still has to be written. Staging is a transaction boundary. A whole document's claims land together or not at all, so a document that failed halfway through extraction contributes nothing rather than contributing a misleading subset. A half-ingested filing must never look like a complete one, because a lawyer reading a complete-looking filing draws conclusions from what is absent. Promotion moves signed-off staged claims to live. Claims still awaiting review stay staged — that is the gate working, not a partial failure. Retraction, and why it cascades Withdrawing a fact is not deletion. It marks the fact superseded from a moment in time, and it transitively withdraws every conclusion that rested on it. Withdrawing a fact. Anything inferred from it is withdrawn at the same time, so no conclusion outlives the reason it was drawn. The failure this prevents is silent, which is why it is an enforced invariant rather than a convention. Retract the extraction that said counsel represents a party, leave the conflict flag standing, and the graph now asserts a conflict whose stated basis has been withdrawn. Every "why do you believe this?" answer for that flag cites a retracted premise — which is exactly the question the system exists to answer well, answered badly, on the highest-stakes fact in the graph. Because nothing is deleted, a reading of the graph as of a date before the retraction still shows the fact and still shows the conflict flag it supported. That is not a quirk; it is the requirement. "What did the file show when we advised?" has to stay answerable after a correction, and that is what transaction time is for. An audit record of one retraction keeps the root separate from the cascade, because they are different events to a reader: one person decided one thing, and a number of conclusions fell as a consequence. Collapsing them would misreport a single decision as many decisions. Reviewing everything anyway A firm that wants to review even the mechanically-confirmed claims can. A governance setting sends those to the queue as well, and the interface warns what will happen: Pattern-matched facts now require review. The queue will grow considerably. The reasonable use is onboarding — a firm building confidence in the extractors, for a period, with the intention of turning it off. Left on permanently it reintroduces exactly the queue-size problem the design exists to avoid, and the outcome is bulk approval. Not built yet That setting is stored, validated, and warned about when changed, but nothing reads it at extraction time. Turning it on currently changes nothing about what enters the queue. Review state is still derived purely from the epistemic class. The same is true of the setting that would force review for governing relationships regardless of class: it is defined and documented, and no code consults it. Since the extractor already refuses to mark anything but a presence relationship as confirmed, every governing relationship from a document already goes to review by construction — so the setting is currently redundant rather than broken. It would matter if a system-of-record importer ever declared governing relationships directly.

title: Governance settings
summary: Trust thresholds, kill switches, model choices and retrieval limits, set per firm and changeable without a redeployment. One relationship between two of them is enforced in code rather than merely documented, and it is the most important thing on this page.

headings.text: Why these are settings and not constants
A test that keeps the help text readable

body: Using it Governance settings Trust thresholds, kill switches, model choices and retrieval limits, set per firm and changeable without a redeployment. One relationship between two of them is enforced in code rather than merely documented, and it is the most important thing on this page. src/governance.py · src/api/routes_governance.py Why these are settings and not constants Every value here could have been a constant in the source. Two reasons it is not. A firm onboarding a new practice area will want a different confidence threshold from the one that suits its established work — more cautious in an unfamiliar area, and the caution has to be adjustable by the person accountable for it rather than by a developer. And a model deprecation should be a settings change, not a release. When a model is retired, the alternative to a setting is an emergency deployment on somebody else's timetable. Defaults come from the environment; overrides are stored per firm and survive a restart. The cap/floor invariant Two settings and the relationship between them: Setting Default What it does min_confidence_floor 0.80 Facts scoring below this do not inform answers. They stay visible in the review queue and the audit trail — this gates retrieval, not storage. model_confidence_cap 0.79 The highest confidence any model-extracted interpretation may carry, regardless of what the model says about its own certainty. The cap must stay strictly below the floor. That gap of 0.01 is the entire mechanism, and what it buys is this: an unreviewed model interpretation sits below the retrieval threshold by construction, so it cannot shape an answer even if the review gate were bypassed entirely. Bypassed by what? By a bug. By a route written later that forgets to check. By a data import path nobody has thought of. The review gate is one mechanism; the confidence gap is a second, independent one, and both have to fail before an unapproved interpretation reaches a user. The trap the invariant catches An administrator decides the system is too cautious and lowers the floor from 0.80 to 0.70, to get answers to more questions. The cap is still 0.79. The floor is now 0.70. Every unreviewed model interpretation in the graph — capped at 0.79, therefore above 0.70 — is suddenly eligible to shape answers. Nothing was approved. Nobody reviewed anything. One number moved, the review queue's entire purpose was silently voided, and no error occurred anywhere. The system refuses the change. It returns an error explaining exactly why, in words meant to be shown to the administrator directly: model_confidence_cap (0.79) must stay below min_confidence_floor (0.7). The gap is what keeps an unreviewed model assertion out of answers even if the review gate is bypassed; closing it removes that guarantee. To genuinely lower the floor, the cap has to be lowered first, deliberately, as a separate act. The administrator has to state that they intend the consequence. This is why the coupling is enforced in code rather than written in a runbook. A documented invariant is a hope. And critically, a rejected change does not half-apply: validation runs on a candidate copy of the settings, and a refusal leaves the live settings untouched rather than in a state where the floor moved and the cap did not. The application's own explanation of the cap, shown next to the control: The highest confidence an AI-extracted fact may claim. Kept just below the confidence floor on purpose, so an AI claim can never influence an answer until a person has approved it. The system will not let you raise this to or above the floor. Trust thresholds min_confidence_floor — default 0.80 How certain the system must be before a fact is used in an answer. Facts below it still appear in the review queue; they just do not influence results. Raising it makes answers more conservative and more likely to leave a question unanswered — which is often the correct outcome, and is always a better one than a confident wrong answer. model_confidence_cap — default 0.79 Covered above. Note that a model's stated certainty is not treated as evidence at any point: the cap is applied to whatever it reports, and the extractor does not read the model's confidence for presence claims at all. auto_assert_deterministic — default on Whether mechanically-confirmed facts go live without review. Switching it off sends them to the queue too — slower, but a reasonable posture during onboarding while a firm builds trust in extraction. Not enforced yet Stored, validated, and warned about when changed. Nothing reads it at extraction time, so turning it off does not currently change what enters the queue. require_review_for_governing — default on Force review for the relationships that carry legal consequence — who represents whom, who is adverse to whom, privilege, deadlines — regardless of how the fact was reached. Belt and braces for the cases where a wrong answer is an exposure rather than an embarrassment. Not enforced yet, and currently redundant No code consults this setting. In practice it is redundant today: the extractor refuses to mark anything but a presence relationship as mechanically confirmed, so every governing relationship read from a document already goes to review by construction. It would begin to matter if a system-of-record importer ever declared governing relationships directly, since those would otherwise auto-assert. Kill switches block_ungoverned_queries — default off Refuse tier-4 model-generated SQL entirely. Governed metrics and graph traversal keep working. Refusals are recorded — the firm, the user, the question, the reason, the time — so an administrator can see what people are trying to ask. Treat that log as a backlog rather than an incident report. A question people keep asking is a governed metric waiting to be written. See the kill switch. Fully wired. A firm that turns this on gets the refusal and the audit entry today, with a message written to be shown to a lawyer rather than a developer. block_model_extraction — default off Stop calling the model extractor. Documents still upload, parse, split and index for search, so their text remains findable; no facts are proposed from them. Wired — ingest checks it and reports why extraction did not run. Stale help text The wording next to this control still says "Pattern-based extraction continues, so citations and docket numbers are still picked up", and the same claim appears in the setting's own code comment. That is left over from before the pattern-matching extractor was deleted. There is no pattern-based extraction any more, so switching this on stops all fact extraction from documents. The behaviour is correct; the explanation is out of date. Models Four model choices, each changeable without a release. Setting Used for query_model Interpreting questions and generating SQL. extraction_model Reading documents and proposing facts. enrichment_model Writing descriptions for database tables and columns. A smaller, cheaper model is usually enough. embedding_model Converting document text into vectors for similarity search. Changing the first three is routine, and safe because every fact records the specific versioned producer that created it. Old facts keep citing the model that made them; new ones cite the new model. The generations do not blur. The embedding model is a data migration, not a setting Changing it is not like changing the others. Existing vectors were produced by the previous model, and a similarity search across two generations of embeddings is not an error — it is silently meaningless. Nothing fails. Search quality degrades and no signal says so. The interface warns and requires an explicit re-processing of every document. The warning is in capitals in the product's own help text, which is unusual for this codebase and deliberate. The vector width is part of the same problem: a similarity search across two different dimensionalities is not an error either, for the same reason and with the same lack of symptom. Vocabulary ontology_domain — default legal Which vocabulary of entities, relationships and rules this firm uses. The platform is domain-agnostic; the legal pack is simply the default. A healthcare pack ships alongside it. enforce_closed_vocabulary — default on Reject governing relationships the vocabulary does not define. The product's explanation is the clearest statement of the stakes anywhere in the interface: Reject relationships the ontology does not define. This is what stops the same idea being recorded five different ways — if that happens, a conflict check can return no results and look like a clean report. Strongly recommended on. Switching it off produces a warning to the same effect. See the conflict-check failure for the full worked example. Not enforced yet The setting is stored and warned about. The closed-vocabulary check itself is unconditional in the assertion builder — validation happens against the vocabulary the pack supplies, and no code path consults this flag to decide whether to skip it. In effect the protection is always on, which is the safe direction for the discrepancy to run. Retrieval vector_top_k — default 20 How many document passages to retrieve before expanding into the graph. Must be at least 1. graph_expand_depth — default 2, range 1 to 5 How many relationship hops to follow out from a retrieved passage. Two is usually right; more pulls in weakly related matters. The range is enforced with a stated reason — deeper traversals fan out badly — and the number of paths grows roughly exponentially with depth, so a depth of 5 on a well-connected entity retrieves most of the firm. Both are read by the resolver and genuinely take effect. How a change is applied A settings update is a partial patch, and the sequence is deliberate: Unknown field names are rejected outright. A typo in a setting name silently doing nothing is how a firm ends up believing a control is on when it is not. The patch is merged onto a candidate copy and validated there. A rejected change cannot leave the live settings half-updated. A refusal returns the validation message directly to the administrator. These messages are written to be read by a person accountable for the setting, not by a developer reading a log. Warnings are returned alongside a successful change where the change is safe but consequential — an embedding model swap, disabling the closed vocabulary, disabling auto-assertion. Who changed it and when are recorded on the settings themselves. Governance changes require an administrator. That is checked separately from the tenant check, since a firm's ordinary users may read their firm's settings without being able to change them. A test that keeps the help text readable Every setting has plain-language help text written for a lawyer-administrator rather than a data engineer — "will not be used in answers" rather than "excluded from the retrieval candidate set". There is a test asserting that no jargon leaks into it. That is an unusual thing to test, and it is there because help text decays: the person who understands a setting best is the person least able to notice that their explanation of it has become incomprehensible. A test is the only thing that holds the line. These documents reuse that wording deliberately, so the tooltip in the product and the explanation here cannot drift apart.

title: Loading the demo data
summary: An empty LexGraph cannot demonstrate anything, because the whole point of the system is what happens when facts from different documents meet. Five matters ship with it for that reason, and they are deliberately entangled.

headings.text: What to look for once it has loaded

body: Using it Loading the demo data An empty LexGraph cannot demonstrate anything, because the whole point of the system is what happens when facts from different documents meet. Five matters ship with it for that reason, and they are deliberately entangled. Getting it in The documents are committed to the repository as sample/legal-demo.zip. Download that file, unzip it, and upload the PDFs through Documents, then Upload — the same screen a lawyer uses for anything else. They ship as a plain zip rather than a fixture for that reason: uploading them by hand exercises the path a real user takes, so nothing about the demo is special-cased. Doing it one document at a time is also the better way to watch it, because you can stop after four and see what changes when the fifth arrives. Set the matter on each upload Every filename begins with its matter reference, and that is what belongs in Attach to matter: NTL-2026-0114 for the three NTL- files, MBC-2024-0431 for the facility agreement, HAL-2025-0092 for the authority note. The field accepts typed text as well as a selection, because a matter is derived from the documents filed under it and therefore has nothing to select until its first document is in. Both things this data exists to show are cross-matter. Filing everything under one reference, or leaving it all unassigned, removes precisely what there is to look at. An administrator can load all five at once with Admin, then Load sample data, which reads the same zip from the server. The pipeline is identical either way. They are not seeded facts Each page is rasterised, transcribed by a vision model, split into chunks that keep their character offsets, embedded, and read for claims. Nothing is written into the graph directly. That distinction is the reason to load them at all. Every assertion that appears afterwards resolves to a page and a verbatim sentence on the Provenance screen, because it was genuinely read out of a document rather than declared by a fixture. A seeded demo would show the screens working and prove nothing about the system behind them. What is in them Three matters across five documents: Matter Document What it puts in the graph NTL-2026-0114 Engagement letter The client, the adverse party, and a scope exclusion — an engagement that is narrower than the client might assume. NTL-2026-0114 Advice on prospects Reliance on an authority, The Aquitaine [2019]. NTL-2026-0114 Conflict memorandum An ethical screen, with the reason recorded. MBC-2024-0431 Facility agreement Meridian as a client here, and a shareholder of the adverse party in the matter above. HAL-2025-0092 Authority note The Marisol [2025] overruling The Aquitaine. What to look for once it has loaded Two things become true that were not true of any single document, and neither is visible to a reader of one file: A conflict. Meridian is a client in one matter and a shareholder of the adverse party in another. No document says this. It is what the graph says once both are in it, which is why conflict checking is cross-matter by definition and why tenants get one graph rather than one per matter. A stale authority. Advice in the first matter rests on The Aquitaine, and a document filed under a different matter records that it has been overruled. The advice was correct when written. That is exactly the case bitemporal fields exist to express: the world changed, not the record of it. Both facts arrive as INFERRED , so each carries the proof tree that produced it. Follow it and you reach the two documents and the sentences in them, which is the answer to why does the system believe this in its concrete form. A question worth asking first Ask "are there any conflicts on the Northern Trade matter?" before loading the fifth document, then again afterwards. The answer changes, and the citation shows which document changed it. Starting again Admin, then Reset takes the derived layers away: the graph, the search index, ingest job history, and the cached catalog schemas. It ticks what to remove, so a wipe can be partial. None of that touches S3. The bucket is the source of truth, so Replay rebuilds every document from it and Scan catalog rebuilds the schemas from Glue. A bad extraction run is a re-run, not a data-loss event. Metric definitions are the exception They are kept by default, and deleting them needs the box ticked and a separate confirmation. Everything else in a reset has an upstream source that can regenerate it; a metric was authored by a person in the application and has none. Nothing rebuilds it, so the warning says so in those words rather than asking "are you sure". Changing what they say The PDFs are generated by sample/generate_demo_pdfs.py, and the zip it produces is committed so that downloading the demo needs nothing installed. Edit the script and re-run it to change what the demo asserts. .venv/bin/python sample/generate_demo_pdfs.py Keep the matter reference at the front of each filename. That is where the matter is read from, so a document added to the zip needs no code change.

title: Glossary
summary: Every term the system uses, in plain language. The wording here mirrors the help text shown inside the application, so the tooltip a user reads and the explanation here cannot disagree.
body: Reference Glossary Every term the system uses, in plain language. The wording here mirrors the help text shown inside the application, so the tooltip a user reads and the explanation here cannot disagree. ui/src/epistemic.ts (HELP) Terms Additivity Whether a measure may be summed across periods. Fees billed are additive; matter headcount is not — adding it across months produces a number that means nothing. As-of date Reconstructs what the file showed on a chosen date, including facts since retracted. This is the question that matters when someone asks what you knew at the time you advised. Assertion One fact, with everything needed to defend or retract it: the claim itself, how it was reached, by what specific versioned producer, how confident the system is, where it came from, when it was true, when the system learned it, and who signed it off. Every relationship in the graph is one. See The assertion contract. Bitemporal Two clocks. World time is when a fact was true; transaction time is when the system learned it. Keeping both is what makes "what did we know then" answerable. Confidence How sure the system is of this single fact, from 0 to 1. A verified quote is near-certain, because the words were checked; a model's interpretation is capped below the trust floor until someone approves it; an inference can never exceed the weakest fact it rests on. Confidence floor The trust floor for retrieval. Facts scoring below it stay visible in the review queue and the audit trail, but they never shape an answer. Raising it makes the system more cautious and more likely to say it does not know. DECLARED A system of record said so — a case management export, or a scan of the data catalogue. Treat as given. It is true by definition of the source; if it is wrong, the source is wrong. Enters the graph without review. Descriptive relationship A subject-matter tag. The list is open. Sprawl here costs search precision, not a negligence claim. Epistemic class "Epistemic" means "to do with knowledge". The epistemic class of a fact is how the system came to believe it: declared by a system of record, quoted from a document and checked, read into a document by a language model, inferred by a rule, or guessed. Every fact in LexGraph carries one, which is what lets you ask why it is believed. Ethical wall Matters you are walled off from are invisible to you: they do not appear in results, counts, or the graph. A denial always beats a permission, so a broad role cannot defeat a wall. Implemented as two lists on the caller: an allowlist of matters they may see, and a denylist they may not. The denylist is applied second and always wins. You are told how many matters are withheld, never which. The count prevents you drawing a false conclusion from a partial answer; the identities would let you map out what you are walled off from. See Tenancy and ethical walls. EXTRACTED_DET A quoted sentence was found on a named page of the document, and the system checked the words are there. The check is repeatable and says only that the words appear — nothing about what they imply. Anything read into them is a separate claim that waits for review. Enters the graph without review. It does not mean "a pattern matched something". There is no pattern-matching extractor. See How extraction works. EXTRACTED_MODEL Something read into the document rather than merely found in it — that one holding undercuts another, that a clause replaces an earlier one. A judgement, not a check, so it is not yet trusted. This is the only class that waits for a person to approve or reject it, which is what the review queue is for. Governed metric A metric definition that compiles to SQL deterministically. The same question always produces the same SQL, and no language model is involved in generating it. Governing relationship A relationship that drives a decision with legal consequence: conflicts, privilege, deadlines, citation authority. The list is closed, and a proposed fact using anything outside it is rejected when it is written — because a conflict check that misses a synonym looks exactly like a clean conflict check. Grounding Mapping a proposed relationship name onto one the vocabulary knows. Done by exact matching only, with no language model: a model deciding that two relationship names mean the same thing is a schema decision made by a model. See The predicate vocabulary. INFERRED A rule derived this from other assertions rather than reading it anywhere. As trustworthy as its weakest premise, and never more — the system refuses to record an inference more confident than what it rests on. Open the proof tree to see exactly what it rests on. Ingest state Where a document is in the pipeline. Its text becomes searchable as soon as it is parsed, but anything a model read into it waits for review before it can shape an answer. Matter An engagement — a case, transaction, or advisory instruction. The organising unit of legal work; most other entities hang off a matter. Matters are subgraphs inside a firm's graph, not separate graphs, because conflict checking is by definition across matters. Method The specific, versioned thing that produced this fact — for example a named model, a catalogue scan, or a rule with its version. Versioned so that improving it supersedes its old output instead of quietly mixing generations. Page citation The citation for a fact read from a document: the file, the page, and the words themselves. It is deliberately what you would use to check it by hand — open the file at that page and search for the sentence. Any viewer can do that, and it still works after the document is re-processed. Party A person or organisation with an interest in a matter. Clients, counterparties and third parties are all parties. The role is on the relationship, not the entity — the same company can be a client on one matter and adverse on another. Predicate The relationship in the middle of a fact: counsel represents party. LexGraph keeps two vocabularies of them, one closed and one open. See The predicate vocabulary. PREDICTED A statistical guess from the shape of the graph. Nobody asserted it and no document says it. A research hint, never a finding. Excluded from answers entirely unless you explicitly ask to see suggestions. Premise A fact that an inference rests on. Retract a premise and the conclusion drawn from it is retracted too, so a proof tree is never left hanging. Presigned link A short-lived link that lets you open a source document. It is created at the moment you click and is never stored, because a stored link is both an expiring credential — provenance that stops resolving — and a working key to the file sitting in a database. See Provenance. Proof tree The full chain of reasoning behind an inferred fact, unwound to the documents and records at its base. If any step in it is wrong, the conclusion is wrong, and you can see which step. Provenance The record of where a fact came from and how it was arrived at. For a document, the file, page and quote. For a database, the source, table and column. For a derived fact, the premises it rests on. Quote The words from the document, copied exactly. Not a summary: a paraphrase could not be searched for in the original, so a claim whose quote cannot be found on the stated page is refused rather than recorded. Resolution tier Which part of the read path answered the question. The lower the tier, the less of the answer was generated: tier 1 is compiled SQL with no model at all, tier 4 is a model writing SQL against the real schema. Retraction Withdrawing a fact. Anything inferred from it is withdrawn at the same time, so no conclusion outlives the reason it was drawn. Review queue The list of claims awaiting a human decision. Holds only genuine judgement calls, sorted with the least confident first, because that is where a reviewer's attention is worth most. Its most important property is that it is short. See Reviewing claims. Review state Whether a person has signed this off. Derived from how the fact was reached, not chosen: a fact declared by a system of record, or a quote the system confirmed is on the page, goes live directly. Anything a model read into a document, and anything inferred, waits for a person. No ingest path can opt out of review. Source locator Exactly where a fact came from, precise enough to check by hand: for a document, the file, the page and the sentence quoted from it; for a database, the source, table and column. Span fingerprint (span hash) A fingerprint of the quoted words taken when the fact was recorded. If the underlying document is ever replaced, the fingerprint stops matching and the fact is flagged rather than silently drifting. Supersede Facts are never edited or deleted. A correction records a new fact and marks the old one superseded from that moment, so the audit trail stays intact. Tenant One firm. Every read is filtered to it, using the firm identity taken from the verified sign-in token and never from a request parameter. Matters are subgraphs inside a tenant — not separate graphs, because conflict checking is by definition cross-matter. The isolation is logical rather than physical: firms share one graph database and are separated by a filter that one module owns. See Tenancy and ethical walls. Text offsets An internal position within the extracted text, kept only for diagnosis. It does not correspond to a position in the file you would open, so it is not the citation — the file, page and quote are. Safe to ignore. Time grain The coarsest time buckets this metric may be reported in — monthly, quarterly, and so on. Fixed per metric so the same number cannot be quietly re-cut into a period it is not valid for. Ungoverned-query kill switch Refuses any question that no approved governed metric can answer, rather than falling back to model-generated SQL. Governed metrics keep working. Refused questions are logged and make a good backlog of metrics worth defining. Vocabulary pack Which vocabulary of entities, relationships and rules this tenant uses. The platform is domain-agnostic; the legal pack is simply the default. Called an ontology in the code and the interface. Stages a document passes through The wording here also mirrors the application's own. Registered The file is in immutable storage. Nothing has been read from it yet. Fetching Retrieving the file for processing. Parsing Converting the document to text, keeping the page each passage came from so every later claim can cite a page you can turn to. Chunking Splitting the text into passages, each still carrying its page number. Extracting Reading the passages to propose facts. A quote the system can confirm is on the stated page goes live directly; anything read into the text goes to review. Embedding Indexing the passages for search. From here the verbatim text is findable even though its extracted facts are not yet trusted. Staged Proposed facts are written to the graph but held back from answers. Pending review Waiting for a human to approve or reject the model-extracted facts. Live Reviewed and in use. Approved facts can now shape answers.

title: Architecture
summary: Six infrastructure stacks split by how often they change and how much damage a bad deployment does, not by feature. A graph database, a vector search service, and a managed model service. Locally, a container that speaks the same graph language stands in for the managed one.

headings.text: What running it locally actually proved

body: Reference Architecture Six infrastructure stacks split by how often they change and how much damage a bad deployment does, not by feature. A graph database, a vector search service, and a managed model service. Locally, a container that speaks the same graph language stands in for the managed one. cdk/lib/*.ts · docker-compose.yml The data flow One rule governs the whole picture: the uploaded file is the only source of truth, and everything else is a derived index that can be dropped and rebuilt. upload → object storage (immutable, versioned, encrypted) + a job record → Textract (text and layout, with page numbers) → split into passages (page numbers preserved — they become the citation) → model extraction → confirmed presence → live immediately → interpretation → review queue → embed passages → vector search index → stage facts → human review → promote → rules (not built) The consequence of that rule is that a bad extraction run is never a data-loss event. The evidence is untouched; discard the derived facts and run again. That is what made it possible to delete the pattern-matching extractor outright rather than living with it — see How extraction works. Note where the search index sits relative to the review gate. Passages are indexed before review, deliberately: verbatim text is a quote, not a claim, and lawyers expect to search a document the moment it lands. The gate protects the graph, not the search index. Structured sources are treated entirely differently. Their data never moves. Only metadata — tables, columns, metric definitions — enters the graph, and rows are queried in place at the moment a question is asked. The six stacks Split by deploy cadence and blast radius. The organising question is not "which feature does this belong to?" but "what happens when this is redeployed, and how often will that be?" Stack Contents Why separate network Virtual network, subnets, security groups, service endpoints, outbound gateway. Changes rarely, and everything depends on it. data Graph database, vector search, the document and job stores. Holds the only irreplaceable state, and the graph cluster takes around fifteen minutes to create. auth User directory and the authorisation policy store. Deleting a user directory is unrecoverable. It gets its own blast radius. app The containerised API — control plane, serving, workers — behind a load balancer. Redeployed constantly. Keeping it separate means a routine release cannot touch the graph. mcp The agent tool server, on a managed agent runtime. A different runtime with its own constraints, notably on which availability zones it supports. web Content delivery network in front of the browser application. Static assets on a different release cadence from the API. For comparison, the AWS reference implementation this borrows ideas from uses sixteen. What was dropped, and why, is recorded in the project's own decision log — mostly enterprise catalog governance that a per-firm tenancy model does not need, a SPARQL federation layer that suits a table-first system rather than a document-first one, and a code-generation toolchain whose build tax was real and whose benefit at this size was not. The three stores Graph database — Neptune Database Holds the assertions. The choice of Database rather than the Analytics sibling is covered in Tenancy and ethical walls: Analytics has discrete graph resources, which would allow a graph per firm, but each carries a minimum capacity floor with no automatic scaling, making it a per-customer deployment shape rather than multi-tenant software. The instance class deployed is the smallest burstable one — free-tier eligible for a fixed number of hours, and explicitly not production-grade. It is a context parameter rather than a constant, so raising it does not require a code change. It should be raised before any load test. Two properties of this database shape the code more than they look: There is no schema DDL. No uniqueness constraints, no explicit indexes — it indexes everything automatically. So every constraint the codebase defines is applied in local development and skipped in deployment. That is a real divergence, not a shim: a uniqueness constraint that catches a duplicate locally will not catch it when deployed, which is why uniqueness is enforced by content-addressed identifiers instead of by the database. Authentication is by network identity rather than a password, so there is no graph credential to leak or rotate. Vector search — OpenSearch Serverless Holds passage embeddings for similarity search, and would also provide keyword search. Two stores rather than one is a deliberate consequence: the reference architecture from AWS reached the same conclusion, because the graph database has no full-text search of its own. Two infrastructure notes recorded during the build, both non-obvious: Access requires two separate grants, not one. An identity policy allowing API access is insufficient on its own; a separate data access policy must name the principal. Without it you get a permission error with no indication that a second half is missing. It lives in the app stack rather than the data stack because it names the application's task role, and the tool attaches policy to the stack owning the role. Standby replicas are enabled because with a minimum capacity of zero there is no floor to double, so an idle collection bills nothing either way and the redundancy is free. Not built yet No adapter has been written against this service. The container is defined for local use and the endpoint setting is read, but embeddings are currently held in process and lost on restart. Embedding calls still require real model-service credentials. Models — Amazon Bedrock Provides the extraction model, the query model, the enrichment model and the embedding model. All four are governance settings rather than constants, so a deprecation is a settings change rather than a release. See Governance settings. One small operational detail worth recording because it cost time: the newest models reject a temperature parameter outright. Sending a temperature of zero in the interest of reproducibility failed every extraction with a validation error, which is worse than not pinning it. The parameter is omitted by default. One image, two entry points The agent tool server runs the same container image as the API, entered at a different module. That is the important decision in that stack, and the reason is a governance one rather than an operational one. A tool that answered a question differently from the equivalent web request would mean two implementations of governance — and the tool implementation is the one nobody audits. Same image, same scoping module, same vocabulary gate. The managed runtime validates the caller's token before any of this code runs, so a tool call arrives carrying the same verified firm identity a web request does. There is no service-account path into the graph. Authorisation Sign-in is handled by a managed user directory; the firm identity is a claim in the verified token and is never read from a request parameter. The identifier that appears in a URL path exists for routing and readability — it is validated against the token claim, and a mismatch is refused. Matter-level access uses a policy language whose defining property, for this system, is that a forbid overrides any permit. That is what makes an ethical wall undefeatable by a broad role. See why a denial beats a permission. One infrastructure trap worth recording. The tool runtime and the application share a single role trusted by two service principals, rather than one assuming the other. Assumption would require a trust relationship pointing back from the tool stack to the application stack, which is a circular dependency between stacks. A related trap: the deployment tool attaches policy statements to whichever stack owns the role, so grants written in the tool stack silently emit into the application stack's template and deploying the tool stack alone would not apply them. They are written in the application stack for that reason. Not built yet No authorisation policies have been authored. The authorisation context has the right shape — a list of permitted matters and a list of forbidden ones — and the deny-wins logic is implemented and tested. The policies that would populate it do not exist, and whether the managed policy service supports the override pattern the design depends on is recorded as an open question. The availability zone constraint Do not simplify the network stack The agent runtime supports only a subset of availability zones in the target region. The vector search service's private endpoint supports a different subset. The virtual network must be pinned to the intersection of the two. Zone names are shuffled per account, so the intersection can only be resolved against the account being deployed to — which is why the zone list is currently unset, and is one of two things that must be resolved before any deployment. Left unset, the deployment tool picks the first two zones, which may not be in the intersection. The symptom is a deployment that breaks for a reason with no obvious connection to networking. The second pre-deployment blocker is that the user directory is currently configured to be destroyed when its stack is removed. That must become retain before the first real firm is onboarded: there is no import path back for a deleted user directory. Cost shape Roughly $135–190 per month at idle. Two things dominate, and the larger one is surprising: The graph database bills continuously with no scale-to-zero — free for an initial allowance of instance-hours, then around $50 a month. The nine private network endpoints cost around $65 a month, which is more than the application containers. They are the first thing to remove from a throwaway environment, at the cost of routing that traffic through the outbound gateway instead. Local development Local development uses Neo4j in a container in place of the managed graph database. This works because both speak openCypher over the same protocol, so the same client code runs against either without a compatibility layer. The compose file defines the graph database, a vector search container behind an optional profile, the API, the tool server behind another profile, and the browser application. docker-compose up -d neo4j ENVIRONMENT=local AUTH_DEV_BYPASS_TENANT=dev-tenant \ GRAPH_URI=bolt://localhost:7687 GRAPH_USER=neo4j GRAPH_PASSWORD=... \ .venv/bin/python -m uvicorn src.api.app:app --port 8010 The development authentication bypass is gated twice — once when configuration is validated, and again at request time — because a bypass that is only checked at startup is a bypass that survives a configuration change. Two differences from deployment are worth knowing. Constraints and indexes are applied locally and skipped when deployed, as described above. And the port the container listens on is fixed at 8000 because the agent runtime's protocol contract requires it, so the API uses the same port and local matches deployed. What running it locally actually proved A local run against a real filing confirmed several of the guarantees on these pages end to end, and it is worth recording which, because a passing unit test and a working system are different claims: Provenance was byte-exact against the original document. Re-ingesting identical bytes changed nothing — content-addressed identifiers collapsed the duplicate. A cross-firm read returned 404, and staging another firm's fact was refused at the contract boundary rather than at the web layer. A walled user saw a subset, and a direct probe by identifier was refused with a message that did not reveal a wall exists. The cap/floor invariant held over HTTP — raising the floor succeeded; lowering it into the model cap returned an error with the explanation. The kill switch refused an ungoverned question with a message written for a lawyer. Why the local run mattered Two bugs surfaced in that run that several hundred green unit tests had not. Both came from a whitespace pattern matching newlines, so a run of title-case words walked across a line break: a plaintiff name absorbed the entire court header above it, and a defendant name absorbed the docket line below it. Either would fork the party entity so it never matched the same party elsewhere in the graph — which makes a conflict check under-report silently. That is the failure this whole system is built to prevent, arriving through a line-wrapping detail. Both are fixed, with regression tests covering realistic multi-line filings and asserting that entity identifiers stay stable across layouts. The code those bugs lived in has since been deleted along with the pattern-matching extractor. The lesson has not: entity identity is the thing to test hardest, because getting it wrong produces a reassuring answer. State of the build Around 6,000 lines of Python, six infrastructure stacks that synthesise cleanly, and twelve interface pages. The test suite runs 601 tests, of which 595 pass and 6 fail — all six in the agent tool server's own tests, and two of those are a test-isolation problem (a session manager that cannot be started twice in one process) rather than a product defect. The rest of the suite is green. The largest functional gaps, repeated here in one place: No graph writer. Facts live in an in-process store and are lost on restart. No reasoning engine, so no derived facts and no proof trees in practice. No query executor, so governed metrics return SQL rather than numbers. No model-backed SQL generator, so tier 4 always declines. No vector store adapter, so embeddings are in process. No authorisation policies authored. Nothing deployed. The infrastructure has been synthesised and never applied.
